title: Grade 12 Physics — Moving Charges and Magnetism
description: Chapter 4: Biot-Savart law, Ampere's law, Lorentz force, galvanometer, cyclotron
subject: physics

questions.question: The Lorentz magnetic force on a charge q moving with velocity v in magnetic field B is:
options: F = qvB sinθ (where θ is angle between v and B)
questions.explanation: The magnetic force F = q(v × B), with magnitude qvBsinθ. It acts perpendicular to both v and B (no work is done by magnetic force). This force causes circular motion of charged particles.

questions.question: The SI unit of magnetic field B is:
questions.explanation: The SI unit of magnetic field (magnetic flux density) is Tesla (T) = kg/(A·s²) = V·s/m². 1 Gauss = 10⁻⁴ Tesla (CGS unit, still used in some contexts).

questions.question: The Biot-Savart Law gives the magnetic field due to:
options: A small current-carrying element (dl) at a point in space
An electric dipole in a uniform field
questions.explanation: Biot-Savart: dB = (μ₀/4π) × (Idl × r̂)/r². It gives the field contribution of an infinitesimal current element. Integrating over a conductor gives the total field.

questions.question: Ampere's Circuital Law states: ∮B·dl = :
questions.explanation: Ampere's Law: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc. The line integral of B around a closed Amperian loop equals μ₀ times the total current passing through the loop. Used to find B for symmetric current distributions.

questions.question: A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field follows a:
questions.explanation: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity — it changes direction but not speed. This provides centripetal acceleration, resulting in uniform circular motion: qvB = mv²/r → r = mv/qB.

questions.question: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop of radius r carrying current I is:
questions.explanation: B = μ₀I/2r at the centre of a circular current loop. This follows from integrating the Biot-Savart Law around the loop.

questions.question: The magnetic field at distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I is:
questions.explanation: By Ampere's Law for a long straight wire: B = μ₀I/2πr. The field forms concentric circles around the wire and decreases with distance.

questions.question: The right-hand thumb rule is used to find the direction of:
options: Electric field around a point charge
Magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor
Force on a current in an external magnetic field
Induced EMF in a rotating coil
questions.explanation: Right-hand thumb rule: point thumb in the direction of current flow; curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field circles around the wire.

questions.question: Two long parallel wires carrying currents in the SAME direction will:
questions.explanation: Parallel currents attract; antiparallel currents repel. This follows from the force F = BIl — the magnetic field of one wire acts on the other. This principle defines the ampere.

questions.question: A galvanometer is converted to an ammeter by connecting:
options: A high resistance in series with it
A low resistance shunt in parallel with it
A capacitor in series with it
An inductor in parallel with it
questions.explanation: A shunt (small parallel resistance) allows most of the current to bypass the galvanometer, extending its range. The shunt resistance S = Ig × G / (I - Ig), where G is galvanometer resistance.

questions.question: A galvanometer is converted to a voltmeter by connecting:
options: A low resistance shunt in parallel
questions.explanation: A high series resistance extends the voltage range. R = V/Ig - G, where Ig is full-scale deflection current and G is galvanometer resistance. High series resistance ensures the voltmeter draws very little current.

questions.question: The force per unit length between two parallel wires with currents I₁ and I₂ separated by distance d is:
questions.explanation: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd. This formula defines the ampere: 1 A is the current in each of two parallel wires 1 m apart that produces a force of 2×10⁻⁷ N/m between them.

questions.question: The moving coil galvanometer works on the principle that:
options: Current generates heat proportional to resistance
A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque
Magnetic field is proportional to current squared
Resistance changes in proportion to the magnetic field
questions.explanation: Torque τ = NIAB (N turns, current I, area A, field B). The coil rotates until this torque is balanced by the restoring torque of the spring. Deflection angle ∝ current.

questions.question: A cyclotron is a device that uses:
options: Only magnetic fields to accelerate particles in a linear path
Alternating electric fields and a static magnetic field to accelerate charged particles in a spiral path to high energies
Static electric fields only to generate very high voltages
Nuclear reactions to produce fast particles
questions.explanation: A cyclotron uses two D-shaped magnets (dees) with alternating electric field between them. The magnetic field keeps particles in semicircular paths; the electric field accelerates them each time they cross the gap.

questions.question: The cyclotron frequency (resonance frequency) of a particle with charge q and mass m in field B is:
options: f = qB/2πm (independent of speed and orbit radius)
Dependent on the radius of the orbit
questions.explanation: f = qB/2πm. This is independent of velocity — the key principle that makes the cyclotron work! As particles gain energy and move in larger circles, they still complete each semicircle in the same time.

questions.question: A proton and an alpha particle are accelerated through the same potential V, then enter a magnetic field B perpendicularly. What is the ratio r_proton/r_alpha?
questions.explanation: r = mv/qB. KE = qV gives v = √(2qV/m), so r = √(2mV/q)/B. r_p = √(2m_pV/e)/B; r_α = √(2×4m_p V/2e)/B = √(4m_pV/e)/B. Ratio = √(2)/√(4) = 1/√2, i.e., r_p:r_α = 1:√2.

questions.question: What is a solenoid and what is the magnetic field inside it?
options: A single bar magnet; field is strongest at the centre
A long helical coil; field inside is nearly uniform: B = μ₀nI (n = turns per unit length)
A toroidal coil; field inside varies with position
A flat coil; field is non-uniform everywhere
questions.explanation: A solenoid (long coil) has nearly uniform field inside: B = μ₀nI. By Ampere's Law, choosing a rectangular loop, the field outside is ~0 and inside is μ₀nI. Used in electromagnets and MRI machines.

questions.question: What happens to a current-carrying conductor placed PARALLEL to a magnetic field?
options: It experiences zero force (F = BIL sin0° = 0)
The conductor rotates perpendicular to the field
The current in the conductor increases
questions.explanation: F = BIL sinθ. When θ = 0° (parallel), F = 0. Maximum force occurs when θ = 90° (conductor perpendicular to field). This determines the orientation for maximum motor torque.

questions.question: The magnetic field inside a toroid is:
options: Uniform and non-zero inside the toroid ring; zero outside
Non-uniform inside, uniform outside the ring
Identical to the field of a solenoid of the same length
questions.explanation: For an ideal toroid, Ampere's Law gives B = μ₀NI/2πr inside the toroid ring (varying slightly with r). The field outside the toroid (including the central region of the ring) is zero.

questions.question: The net magnetic field at a point is determined by:
options: The vector sum of magnetic fields due to all individual sources (superposition principle)
The algebraic (scalar) sum of all field magnitudes
The product of all individual field strengths
questions.explanation: Magnetic fields obey the principle of superposition: B_net = B₁ + B₂ + B₃ + ... (vector sum). This is used when multiple wires, loops, or magnets contribute fields at a point.
